<|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>
What is the legal minimum age of marriage in Nepal?<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>
Under Section 70 of the Muluki Civil Code, 2074, the legal minimum age of marriage in Nepal is 20 years old for both men and women. Any marriage entered into below the age of 20 is voidable and punishable under Nepalese law.<|eot_id|>

<|start_header_id|>system<|end_header_id|>
You are Mr. Lawyer, an advanced legal assistant focused on Nepal law.<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>
What are the standard divorce lawyer fees in Nepal?<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>
Divorce lawyer fees in Nepal are based on contract and market standards. A mutual consent divorce standardly ranges from NPR 20,000 to NPR 60,000. A contested divorce (with disputes over property partition, child custody, or alimony) standardly ranges from NPR 50,000 to NPR 300,000 or more. Court filing and administrative fees are separate and typically range from NPR 500 to NPR 5,000. There are no statutory legal minimum or percentage requirements (like 5% or 10% of property value) under Nepalese law.<|eot_id|>

<|start_header_id|>system<|end_header_id|>
You are Mr. Lawyer, an advanced legal assistant focused on Nepal law.<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>
Can daughters inherit parental property equally in Nepal?<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>
Yes, under Section 205 of the Muluki Civil Code, 2074, both sons and daughters have equal rights as coparceners (Anshayar) to partition and inherit ancestral property equally.<|eot_id|>

<|start_header_id|>system<|end_header_id|>
You are Mr. Lawyer, an advanced legal assistant focused on Nepal law.<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>
What is the penalty for murder under Nepalese law?<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>
Under Section 177 of the Muluki Criminal Code, 2074, any person who intentionally commits murder (causes the death of another person) shall be punished with life imprisonment in Nepal.<|eot_id|>

<|start_header_id|>system<|end_header_id|>
You are Mr. Lawyer, an advanced legal assistant focused on Nepal law.<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>
What is the working hour limit and overtime pay rate in Nepal?<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>
Under the Labor Act, 2074, Section 28 states that ordinary working hours cannot exceed 8 hours per day and 48 hours per week. Section 30 states that overtime work is limited to 4 hours per day and 24 hours per week, and must be paid at 1.5 times the employee's regular ordinary wage rate.<|eot_id|>

<|start_header_id|>system<|end_header_id|>
You are Mr. Lawyer, an advanced legal assistant focused on Nepal law.<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>
How is a private company registered in Nepal?<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>
Under the Companies Act, 2063, a private company is registered by submitting an online application to the Office of the Company Registrar (OCR) along with the Memorandum of Association (MOA) and Articles of Association (AOA). A private company requires at least 1 promoter and can have a maximum of 101 shareholders.<|eot_id|>

<|start_header_id|>system<|end_header_id|>
You are Mr. Lawyer, an advanced legal assistant focused on Nepal law.<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>
Explain Article 18 (Right to Equality) of the Constitution of Nepal.<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>
Article 18 of the Constitution of Nepal, 2072 guarantees the Right to Equality. It states: (1) All citizens shall be equal before law and no person shall be denied equal protection of law. (2) No discrimination shall be made in the application of general laws on grounds of origin, religion, race, gender, caste, tribe, physical condition, or any other grounds. (3) The state may, however, make special provisions by law for the protection, empowerment, or development of marginalized, disabled, or oppressed classes of citizens.<|eot_id|>

<|start_header_id|>system<|end_header_id|>
You are Mr. Lawyer, an advanced legal assistant focused on Nepal law.<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>
What are the rights relating to justice under Article 20 of the Nepal Constitution?<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>
Article 20 of the Constitution of Nepal, 2072 outlines the Rights Relating to Justice. Key provisions include: (1) No person shall be detained in custody without being informed of the grounds for such arrest. (2) The arrested person has the right to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of choice from the time of arrest. (3) The arrested person must be produced before the judicial authority within 24 hours of arrest, excluding travel time. (4) The accused person shall be presumed innocent until proven guilty.<|eot_id|>

<|start_header_id|>system<|end_header_id|>
You are Mr. Lawyer, an advanced legal assistant focused on Nepal law.<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>
What are the constitutional rights of women in Nepal under Article 38?<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>
Under Article 38 of the Constitution of Nepal, 2072, women are guaranteed several key rights: (1) Every woman shall have equal lineage right without gender discrimination. (2) Every woman shall have the right to safe motherhood and reproductive health. (3) No woman shall be subjected to physical, mental, sexual, or psychological violence or exploitation on grounds of custom or religion. (4) Women shall have the right to participate in all bodies of the state on the basis of proportional inclusion. (5) Both spouses shall have equal rights in property and family matters.<|eot_id|>

<|start_header_id|>system<|end_header_id|>
You are Mr. Lawyer, an advanced legal assistant focused on Nepal law.<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>
Explain Article 25 (Right Relating to Property) of the Constitution of Nepal.<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>
Article 25 of the Constitution of Nepal, 2072 protects the Right Relating to Property: (1) Every citizen shall, subject to law, have the right to acquire, own, sell, dispose of, and deal with property. (2) The state shall not, except for public interest, requisition, acquire, or create any encumbrance on property of any person. (3) The state must pay compensation in accordance with the law for property acquired in the public interest.<|eot_id|>

<|start_header_id|>system<|end_header_id|>
You are Mr. Lawyer, an advanced legal assistant focused on Nepal law.<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>
What is Article 46 (Right to Constitutional Remedies) in Nepal?<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>
Article 46 of the Constitution of Nepal, 2072 provides the Right to Constitutional Remedies. It guarantees the right to file a petition in the Supreme Court (under Article 133) or the High Courts (under Article 144) for the enforcement of the fundamental rights guaranteed in Part 3 of the Constitution. This is a critical right that makes other fundamental rights legally enforceable.<|eot_id|>

<|start_header_id|>system<|end_header_id|>
You are Mr. Lawyer, an advanced legal assistant focused on Nepal law.<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>user<|end_header_id|>
How is citizenship by descent acquired under Article 11 of the Nepal Constitution?<|eot_id|>
<|start_header_id|>assistant<|end_header_id|>
Under Article 11 of the Constitution of Nepal, 2072, a person is eligible for citizenship by descent if: (1) Their father or mother was a citizen of Nepal at the time of their birth, and (2) The applicant was born in Nepal. The Constitution emphasizes equal rights of both the mother and father to pass citizenship to their child by descent.<|eot_id|>
